kinds.d: Mechanical model of the Sun, planets and moons, turned by hand, clockwork or motor.

x.d: The first orreries: George Graham's planetary machine, copied and improved by John Rowley for the Earl of Orrery, who gave the device its name.

v.d: made for Charles Boyle, 4th Earl of Orrery

x.d: Orrery after the new planetary model Benjamin Martin devised in 1764; a 1766 example was used at Harvard.
American classroom tellurion showing Sun, Earth, Moon and Venus with seasons, phases and eclipses, made in Michigan since the early 20th century.
x.dt: maple, ebonised, Bakelite or plastic arm · hand-cranked or electric

kinds.d: Hand-held instrument that models the sky, used to find star and Sun positions, the time and latitude.

x.d: Classic astrolabe: a mater holding latitude plates (tympans) under a rotating star map (rete), with a sighting alidade on the back; Greek in origin, refined in the Islamic world.
x.dt: mater · tympans for latitudes · rete · alidade · brass

x.d: Astrolabe usable at any latitude without changing plates, perfected by Ibn al-Sarraj of Aleppo.
Astrolabe adapted for use on a ship's heaving deck; a simplified form was promoted by Prince Henry the Navigator.

kinds.d: Model of the sky made of rings for the celestial equator, ecliptic and other circles around a central Earth or Sun.
Globe showing the stars and constellations on the celestial sphere, usually mounted with meridian and horizon rings.

x.d: Willem Jansz Blaeu's engraved celestial globes from Amsterdam, first based on Tycho Brahe's star catalogue; among the finest of 17th-century Europe.
x.dt: engraved gores · brass meridian · wooden stand

x.d: Georgian library globe from J. & W. Cary of the Strand, the leading British globe makers of the 19th century.
Modern celestial globes from Replogle, the Chicago globe maker founded in 1930.

kinds.d: Pair of rotating discs that show which stars are above the horizon at any date and time for one latitude.

x.d: The best-known British planisphere, set for latitude 51.5° N.
Two-sided planisphere with separate north- and south-facing maps that removes most distortion; first printed in 1976.
Planisphere by Storm Dunlop and Wil Tirion, approved by the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

kinds.d: Small projector that shows the night sky on the ceiling and walls of a room.

x.d: The first home optical planetarium, developed by Takayuki Ohira with Sega Toys in 2005; about 1.7 million sold by 2021.

kinds.d: Double-reflecting hand instrument that measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon for navigation.

x.d: John Hadley's double-reflecting instrument of about 1731 (also found by Thomas Godfrey), the ancestor of the sextant.
German micrometer-drum sextant with a bronze frame, made by Cassens & Plath of Bremen from 1962, often sold through Weems & Plath.
x.dt: bronze frame · black enamel · micrometer drum

x.d: Plastic micrometer-drum sextant sold as a low-cost learner and backup instrument.

brands.d: Michigan maker of the Trippensee planetarium tellurion, separated from Trippensee Manufacturing in 1920; bought by Science First in 1999.
London globe and map makers John and William Cary, the leading British globe producers of the 19th century.
Amsterdam cartographer and globe maker, pupil of Tycho Brahe.
Chicago globe maker founded by Luther Replogle, making Earth, Moon, planet and celestial globes.
British map and atlas publisher whose Philip's planisphere is the best-known in Britain.
Japanese toy maker that developed the Homestar home planetarium with Takayuki Ohira.
Bremen nautical instrument firm founded by Captain Tanne Janssen Cassens, renamed with Theodore Plath in 1908; making its own sextants from 1962.
Californian maker of weather stations and marine instruments, including the plastic Mark 15 sextant.

traditions.d: Tradition of brass astrolabes and treatises in the Islamic world, from al-Fazari in the 8th century to universal and geared astrolabes, later carried on in India.
traditions.tech: cast and engraved brass, stereographic projection of plates, pierced rete
traditions.auth: signed or dated inscriptions; plate latitudes for named places

traditions.d: Latin astrolabe tradition after Gerbert of Aurillac brought the instrument north of the Pyrenees, with treatises by Chaucer and Stöffler.
traditions.tech: engraved brass plates and rete, Latin scales
traditions.auth: Latin inscriptions and star names, maker's signature, plate latitudes

notes: Orrery: 3 archetypes (Graham–Rowley, Benjamin Martin, Trippensee) with the old Trippensee model as a version; Cochranes Orbit and generic Grand Orrery kept in m; modern geared kit orreries not added (no page). Astrolabe: planispheric, universal and mariner's archetypes; Islamic and European traditions from the Wikipedia article. New kinds Armillary sphere (types only, no owned-model page), Celestial globe (Blaeu, Cary, Replogle), Planisphere (Philip's, Chandler Night Sky, Collins; Miller not found), Sextant (Hadley octant, Cassens & Plath, Davis Mark 15; Heath and Tamaya not added, no page). Home planetarium projector: renamed from Planetarium projector; Carl Zeiss Mark V and Universarium IX dropped as professional dome projectors (Megastar likewise excluded); Orzorz dropped; Homestar models became versions of the Sega Toys Homestar archetype.
